Many journalists are relying on the report by the @OAS_official on the Brazilian presidential election runoff to justify why the outcome should be accepted as is. The report does not publish a forensic reconstruction of the processing pause during the Zanin Window and does not address which systems changed, who accessed them, whether result files were replaced, or how independently preserved polling station tallies were reconciled with the final totals.

Its account of continued regional transmission also relies on information supplied by TSE technical staff. The report does not provide the underlying records needed to reconstruct each stage independently. These limits mean the report does not decisively resolve the allegation of manipulation during the Zanin Window.

What needs to happen to have confidence in the integrity of the election, which Lula badly needs if he actually won and he is to have legitimacy to govern, is to preserve the records and commission an independent technical audit with Brazilian and international forensic experts.

In 1591 he secretly married Bess Throckmorton, one of Elizabeth's ladies in waiting, which the Queen regarded as a personal betrayal, and both of them went to the Tower for a month.

He bought his way back with the capture of the Madre de Deus in 1592, a Portuguese carrack whose cargo was worth a staggering amount, and in 1595 he was commissioned to go and find El Dorado.

He went to Guiana, found no golden city, and wrote a book about it that was more persuasive than the evidence warranted. That book is why he kept believing in it for the next twenty years.

Then Elizabeth died, and James I came south from Scotland with one overriding foreign policy goal, which was peace with Spain.

Raleigh was the most famous Spain-hating privateer in England. He was the opposite of everything the new reign wanted.

In 1603 he was accused of involvement in a plot to put Arbella Stuart on the throne. The trial was a disgrace even by the standards of the time. The main evidence was a confession from Lord Cobham, who retracted it and then re-made it, and Raleigh was denied the right to have Cobham brought into court to face him. The prosecutor Edward Coke abused him from the bench.

Raleigh defended himself so well that the trial started turning public opinion in his favour, which is a rare thing for a man already convicted in everyone's mind.

He was condemned, then reprieved at the last moment, and spent the next thirteen years in the Tower.

He also kept telling anybody who would listen that there was a gold mine in Guiana.

items.tx:
Well, another Cardinal has come out with a, shall we say, puzzling take on evangelization.

A few years ago, Cardinal Américo Aguiar, at the time auxiliary bishop of Lisbon, said that he and the other organizers of World Youth Day in his hometown had no interest in converting anyone to Christ.

Now Cardinal Jean-Paul Vesco of Algeria has opined that “the Church is not there to convert” and “Christians should approach other religions through fraternity rather than seeking conversions.” 

Excuse me, but…what?

Last time I checked, the Founder said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you.” Sure sounds like conversion to me.

When St. Paul came to Corinth or Athens or Thessalonica, his purpose was not to listen or to form a discussion group but rather to declare an unnerving message: the euangelion (glad tidings) that Jesus Christ is risen from the dead.

So impassioned is he for this work that he says, “I have become all things to all people, that I might by all means save some. I do it all for the sake of the gospel” (1 Cor. 9:22); and “If I proclaim the gospel, this gives me no ground for boasting, for an obligation is laid on me, and woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel” (1 Cor. 9:16)!

Moreover, the entire thrust of the Second Vatican Council was toward bringing the Light of Christ to the peoples of the world (Lumen Gentium). And this missionary élan has given rise in the last few decades to the idea of a “new evangelization,” which is to say, a fresh declaration of the Lordship of Christ.

Quite obviously, no one thinks that this work of evangelization should be done in a brow-beating, overbearing, or disrespectful manner (proselytization), but for God’s sake, let’s not throw the baby out with the bathwater.

If I really thought that the Church does not exist to bring people to Christ, then I would resign and get an honest job.

items.tx:
This is true everywhere in the West.

Palmer Luckey just launched BlueChip with Qualcomm, a laptop designed and assembled in the United States. The "analysts" told us an American computer would cost $100,000. Luckey says it'll cost about 20% more than a high-end PC. The gap between those two numbers is the size of the lie.

In France, we know this song by heart.

Taxis. In 2008, a government commission proposed opening up taxi licenses. Strikes, highways blocked, and the government backed down within days. A Paris taxi license would eventually resell for over €200,000. Scarcity created by the state turned into private wealth. It took Uber to break it, and in 2014 the government passed a law to try to lock it all back down.

Telecom. In 2005, Orange, SFR and Bouygues were fined €534M for colluding on market share. In 2012, a newcomer called Free launched unlimited plans at €19.99. Prices collapsed. Nobody went bankrupt. We had just been paying a cartel.

Pharmacies. A legal monopoly down to the last box of over-the-counter Tylenol. France's largest supermarket chain has been fighting for over fifteen years for the right to sell it. Still no.

Notaries. Decades of de facto caps on the number of practices. When reform finally opened new offices, they took to the streets.

Driving schools. A startup called Ornikar shows up with a cheaper license path, and the industry drags it into court.

And at the EU level, GDPR and the AI Act: rules that only a company with 200 lawyers can comply with. Exactly the moat incumbents dream of.

The pattern is always the same. Manufacture scarcity through law, call it protection, and tell everyone there's no other way.

What AI is doing right now is exposing the scam run by what I call the pseudo-communist entrepreneurs. People who preach free markets and live off administered rents. Central planning, privatized.

The perfect embodiment is Bill Gates. In 2005, he called people who wanted to loosen intellectual property rules "modern-day communists." The irony is total. In the 90s, Microsoft charged PC makers a license fee on every machine they shipped, whether Windows was installed on it or not. The Justice Department had to ban the practice in 1994. Then came the US antitrust ruling for monopoly abuse, then a €497M fine from Brussels in 2004. The real central planner was him.

This whole economy rests on one thing: production costs were high and opaque, so they could charge you for the license, the toll, the stamp. AI is crushing that cost. Code is heading toward zero. Entry-level legal, accounting and medical expertise is heading toward zero. And when producing something costs almost nothing, a rent can no longer be defended by economics, only by law. That's when everyone sees the machinery naked.

It's going to blow up. And it's going to create insane abundance.

Thank you Palmer Luckey for yesterday.

Two days ago I wrote a thread about geniuses. I think Palmer Luckey has the potential to join Elon Musk in that category within a few years. Oculus at 19, Anduril closing in on $100B, and now he's going after the very idea that the West has forgotten how to build things. You see maybe one trajectory like this per generation.
